summary: Follow-up to the Verdant incident on May 10 where inference latency spiked and some requests failed after an autoscaler regression caused pod churn and KV cache invalidations. Discussed root cause analysis, mitigations applied (rollback, temporary scaling bump, cache warming), longer-term reliability suggestions (rate-limiting, improved alerting, canary rollout for autoscaler changes), and agreed next steps for both teams to validate fixes on staging and schedule a runbook review.
transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-05-14
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Arjun Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM), Priya Singh (Verdant SRE), Daniel Park (Verdant VP Eng), Hannah Lee (Verdant Data Platform), Marcus Reyes (Verdant Backend)

Topics: Incident recap, root cause summary, temporary mitigations, proposed permanent fixes, verification plan, runbook and playbook updates, timeline for follow-ups

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We wanted to do a quick follow-up on the May 10 incident — walk through the RCA we put together and the mitigation steps we applied, and align on next steps. Priya, thanks for being here, hope things are calmer now?

[00:12] Priya Singh: Yeah thanks Maya. Still some follow-up work but overall the rollback we did helped. We did see reduced failures after the 03:30 UTC rollback, but there were a few stragglers until the cache fully warmed.

[00:25] Arjun Patel: Right, quick summary for context — our preliminary RCA shows an autoscaler config regression that reduced the upper bound on pod replicas for the dedicated pool Verdant is on. During a high-throughput window, that led to pod churn; pods terminated and restarted, which invalidated several KV cache entries and caused many cold-starts. Because the request pattern had lots of long-tail sequences, the per-request latency spiked and some requests timed out at the app layer.

[00:50] Daniel Park: When you say "config regression" — is that a Redwood change or a Verdant change? We had not made any scaling changes on our side.

[00:58] Arjun Patel: Good question. The regression originated in a recent autoscaler tweak we pushed to the shared control plane for the dedicated cluster templates. It was intended to tighten down ephemeral scaling to reduce cost during quiet hours but the new threshold logic combined with Verdant's burst pattern resulted in an effective hard cap. We own that — should have caught it in canary.

[01:22] Priya Singh: OK understood. The cache warming bit is... can you explain why cache entries were lost across pod restarts? I thought we had prefix caching to the shared KV store.

[01:30] Arjun Patel: Sure — the KV store is external, but we use a local in-memory prefix cache for hot keys per replica to reduce latency. When pods restart, that in-memory cache is empty until warm. The external KV had the entries, but there was an access path issue under high parallelism; we saw elevated error rates to the external KV (timeouts), which prevented efficient warm-up and caused the exponential backoff in some clients. So it's both the churn and the KV access pressure.

[02:05] Hannah Lee: Any idea why external KV had timeouts? We didn't see similar issues in our other services hitting the same store.

[02:12] Arjun Patel: We're still digging—initially it correlates with a burst of small requests that increased connections and saturated connection pool settings in the KV client we ship in the runtime. That plus the pod churn made retries pile up.

[02:32] Marcus Reyes: Were there any DB-level throttles? We want to know if it's a quota or client pool sizing problem.

[02:38] Arjun Patel: No DB throttles reported from the KV provider — their metrics were within limits. It looks like connection exhaustion on the runtime side. We have a small heap of fixes: increase client pool limits, add circuit breaker around KV calls, and make cache warms more aggressive on startup with backoff jitter to avoid thundering herd.

[02:58] Daniel Park: What about the failures that users saw — were they 5xx from Redwood or did they originate in our app?

[03:05] Arjun Patel: Most of the hits were 504/timeout surfaced by your app proxy because the backend latency exceeded the proxy deadline. Redwood responded with 200s on tokenization and partial streams in some cases but overall it manifested as timeouts on your side. We have a log sample we can share with request IDs.

[03:26] Priya Singh: Please do — request IDs are how we'll stitch traces.

[03:30] Maya Chen: We'll attach the sample logs in the postmortem deck. Quick note on mitigation timeline — the sequence was: alert triggered at 02:18 UTC for elevated 95/99 latency, our on-call SE triaged, identified autoscaler cap at 02:45, we rolled back autoscaler config to the previous version at 03:30 which allowed pods to scale to the previous cap. We then increased temporary replica burst by +30% for 2 hours to let caches warm, and reduced client pool limits after observing high connections — that last tweak was a short-term band-aid.

[03:58] Priya Singh: That matches our timeline. We also implemented a temporary request rate limiter on the ingress to reduce pressure until things settled.

[04:06] Liam O'Connor: Good collaboration there. For longer-term fixes Arjun's proposed: canaries for control-plane changes, autoscaler SLOs with constraints, improved KV client defaults, and runbook updates for handling cache-warm events — is that the right summary?

[04:20] Arjun Patel: Yes. Also we recommend a staged rollback test in your staging to validate the autoscaler thresholds against your traffic shape, and adding a synthetic warm-up traffic for new pods so the local cache gets populated before routing production traffic to them.

[04:36] Daniel Park: Synthetic warmup sounds reasonable. Will that cost us more tokens obviously but better than customer-facing errors.

[04:44] Arjun Patel: Exactly. We can tune the warm-up to be low-cost — short prefix queries, not full long sequences.

[04:52] Priya Singh: On alerts — our alert ran off of 95th/99th latency which tripped late. Could Redwood provide a preemptive signal? Maybe an early warning metric like connection pool saturation or retry rate?

[05:03] Arjun Patel: Yes, we can expose runtime metrics for connection pool usage, KV retry counts, and autoscaler reject counts. We can also add a Slack alert integration into your channel if you want to receive pre-threshold warnings.

[05:15] Hannah Lee: Security question — you mentioned rollback and config changes on the control plane. Were any customer secrets or data touched during this incident?

[05:22] Maya Chen: No, no customer data was exfiltrated. The rollback was a config change and temporary scaling. KMS and customer blobs were unaffected. We'll include an audit log export for the change window in the deck.

[05:34] Daniel Park: Ok good. From a compliance perspective we need those audit logs for SOC2 evidence. Please include the change IDs.

[05:42] Maya Chen: Will do.

[05:45] Priya Singh: For the permanent fix, who owns what? We want to make sure there's clear responsibilities.

[05:52] Arjun Patel: Redwood will own: canary workflow for autoscaler changes, runtime KV client tuning, additional runtime metrics and alerts, and a suggested warm-up implementation. Verdant will own: test validation in staging with synthetic traffic, update ingress timeout thresholds, and runbook updates. We'll collaborate on runbook language.

[06:10] Daniel Park: Sounds fair. Can we get a proposal for the canary plan? Ideally with rollout steps and a quick backout script.

[06:18] Arjun Patel: Absolutely. I'll draft a canary runbook with explicit metrics to watch (KV retry count, connection pool usage, 95th latency, pod churn) and a rollback script that returns the autoscaler to previous template.

[06:30] Marcus Reyes: One more practical ask — can we have an API to pin a higher replica minimum for critical windows? We run nightly ETL that spikes requests.

[06:39] Maya Chen: There is currently a per-customer config to set minimum replicas and burst policies for Dedicated. We'll surface how to set that so Verdant can pin minima during ETL windows.

[06:48] Priya Singh: Great. Also recommend we get a run of the incident in our post-incident playbook to make sure on-call knows the steps.

[06:55] Liam O'Connor: I'll coordinate a tabletop run for the on-call team — schedule options to follow in that runbook invite.

[07:05] Maya Chen: OK let's recap next steps — Maya to send the deck and logs by 5/16, Arjun to send config diffs and canary proposal by 5/18, Priya to share cluster logs by 5/15, Liam to book runbook review for 5/21. Any other asks?

[07:18] Priya Singh: Please include the sample request IDs and any span traces you have. Helps speed our tracing correlation.

[07:25] Arjun Patel: We'll include request IDs and span IDs where available; a few traces are incomplete due to timeouts but we have enough for root cause.

[07:35] Daniel Park: Thank you all. Appreciate Redwood owning the regression. We'll prioritize the staging validation and get back with results.

[07:45] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up in email with the deck and action items.

[07:50] End of call.

References/Attachments: Postmortem deck (link: https://rwd.internal/pm/verdant-may10-postmortem), sample logs (attached), canary proposal (to be shared), runbook draft (to be shared)

Recording notes: Medium-quality transcription; some speaker labels may be slightly off and a few technical terms transcribed imperfectly (e.g., KV vs K-V, autoscaler vs auto-scaler).
